transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I’m here because things in my husband’s family have gotten to where I can’t just keep pretending it’s nothing. His sister—my sister-in-law—she’s been working this whole family business situation, and I mean really working it, so she can get control over the money and push me out of decisions that I should have a say in. 

People keep trying to smooth it over, like, “Oh, that’s just how she is,” or “You’re reading too much into it,” but I know what I’ve been seeing. This hasn’t been just one misunderstanding or one bad conversation. It’s been going on for more than a year now, little things and bigger things, and when you put them all together it’s clear. I came because I’m tired of everyone acting like I’m the problem for noticing it.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to hear or see?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, I hear normal things, like the house settling or people talking in another room, but not voices talking to me or anything like that. And I haven’t seen things that weren’t there, if that’s what you mean.

This isn’t like I’m seeing ghosts or hearing messages. It’s more that I notice what people are doing and saying, and other people act like I’m making too much of it. But no, I’m not hearing or seeing things other people can’t.

Aside from this situation with your husband's family, do you generally find yourself distrustful or suspicious of other people's motives in your life—like friends, coworkers, or other relationships—and has that been the case since you were young?

I don’t know… I mean, I wouldn’t say I walk around suspicious of everybody, if that’s what you mean. I have people I’ve gotten along with fine. I’ve had friends, neighbors, people at church or in stores, and I don’t sit there thinking everyone has some hidden plan.

Since I was young? No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve always been the kind of person who notices things, maybe. If somebody says one thing and does another, I remember it. But I don’t think that’s the same as being suspicious of everyone. This thing with my husband’s family feels different because there are actual things that happened, and it’s been repeated over and over.

So… no, I wouldn’t say this has been my whole life or with everybody. It’s more about this situation and the way they’ve been acting.
Aside from this conflict with your husband's family, has your day-to-day life—your work, friendships, and daily routines—continued pretty much as normal?

For the most part, yes. I mean, I still do my regular things. I go to my quilting group, and I still have choir practice, and I’ve been keeping up with my GED lessons too. I do my senior walks like I always have, because honestly I need that routine or I’d just sit and stew about all this.

It hasn’t made me stop living my life, exactly. It’s more that it’s changed how I feel around my husband’s sister, and which family things I feel comfortable going to. Like if I know she’s going to be there, I think twice, because I don’t want to be put in a position where she can twist things or make me look bad. But with my own day-to-day stuff—my groups, my classes, my walks—I’m still doing those.

If someone showed you clear evidence that your sister-in-law wasn't trying to take control of the money or push you out of decisions, do you think that could change your mind, or does it feel certain to you no matter what?

I mean… if it was truly clear, I suppose anyone would have to look at it. I’m not saying I’m someone who can’t ever be wrong about anything. But the problem is people keep calling things “clear” when really it’s just them smoothing it over, or explaining it away, or saying, “Oh, that’s just how she is,” and expecting me to ignore what I’ve been seeing.

Because this isn’t from one conversation or one little misunderstanding. This has been going on more than a year now, and it’s the same pattern over and over with my husband’s sister—getting herself in the middle of the family business, acting like she should know everything first, making decisions sound like they don’t need to include me, and then if I speak up, suddenly I’m the difficult one. That’s what I came here about. It’s not just a feeling I woke up with one day.

So could something change my mind? I guess if there was real evidence, real actions, not just people saying words to calm me down. But sitting here right now, I know what I’ve seen. I know she’s been trying to get control of the money side of things and push me out of decisions, even if everybody wants to pretend it’s not happening.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, encapsulated delusional belief (>1 year duration) that her sister-in-law is conspiring to seize financial control and exclude her from family decisions. This belief is held with near-certainty, is resistant to counter-evidence, and is circumscribed to this specific persecutory/jealous theme involving one family member. There are no hallucinations, no other psychotic symptoms (disorganized speech, negative symptoms), and no evidence of a pervasive, lifelong pattern of generalized suspiciousness/distrust that would suggest paranoid personality disorder—she explicitly denies broad interpersonal mistrust and reports satisfying friendships and social engagement. Overall functioning (quilting group, choir, GED classes, walking routine) remains intact aside from selective avoidance of the specific relative, consistent with delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia, where functional decline and broader psychotic symptoms would be expected. This presentation meets criteria for Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22.0).
